Issued at 112 PM CST Tue Nov 17 2026

THIS AFTERNOON: Widespread stratus persists through the Tri-state 
area this afternoon, with some thinning on the far western fringes 
in central South Dakota and on the eastern edges along Highway 71. 
Temperatures as expected, started the day already in the upper 40s, 
with not a ton of upwards movement due to this cloud cover. Gusty 
southerly winds continue, with peak winds in the upper 30 mph range 
in most locations. 

TONIGHT: Stratus already in place at sunset will remain in place for 
most of the overnight hours, holding temperatures in the upper 40s 
to lower 50s. Edges that erode late this afternoon may fall a bit 
cooler, but gusty winds overnight will keep mechanical mixing going, 
and the temperature fall won't be all that significant. In fact, low 
temperatures nearly everywhere will stay near their normal high 
temperatures for the date. At this point, we won't set warm 
overnight low temperature records which sit at 50 degrees at HON, 
FSD, and SUX. Winds may remain quite strong through the overnight 
hours as NAEFS/ENS ESAT tables indicate a climatologically 
significant low lvl jet through the Plains sitting at the 99th 
percentile. That said, sustained winds 20-25 mph will persist, with 
some potential for gusts over 40 mph at times. The big limiting 
factor will be the residual stratus hanging on in the 2500 ft AGL 
layer that could limit downward wind transfer. 

WEDNESDAY: We'll start the day with lingering stratus and quite a 
bit of wind. In fact, winds along the higher terrain areas of the 
Buffalo Ridge may need a wind advisory into mid-day. As the upper 
trough moving into the Northern Rockies begins to pivot northeast 
into the Dakotas after daybreak, a weak surface trough, quasi-
dryline, will slide eastward reaching I-29 by later in the 
afternoon. This front should scour out any lingering stratus and 
allow temperatures to surge into the 60s, potentially near 70 in the 
James and central MO river valley area. This front will also bring 
significantly drier air with it, and have deviated from 
deterministic NBM guidance and blended in higher resolution 
HRRR/RAP/RRFS data for dew points in the afternoon Wednesday. While 
winds over most of the CWA will begin to weaken with the arrival of 
this surface trough, a secondary surge of stronger gusts behind the 
true cold front begins to move into south central South Dakota by 
mid- afternoon. It's in this area, where the combination of 20-30% 
RH, temperatures in the upper 60s, and stronger wind gusts continue 
that an elevated fire danger threat will develop through sunset. See 
separate fire weather discussion for further details. 

THURSDAY-FRIDAY: The passage of this secondary trough Wednesday 
night will drop temperatures into Thursday morning, with the 
boundary settling near the I-80 corridor by daybreak Thursday. 
Temperatures Thursday may be slightly cooler in the 50s, but still 
likely 10 degrees above normal. However yet another upper trough 
moves into the Western CONUS on Thursday inducing stronger more 
southerly return flow through the Central Plains during the day. The 
aforementioned cool front will begin to retreat northward Thursday 
evening pushing dew points well above seasonal normals into the 
middle to upper 40s overnight. Widespread stratus returns with this 
boundary into Friday, along with gusty southerly winds. Latest 
deterministic guidance suggests wind gusts as high as the low 40 mph 
range with the NBM 75th percentile indicating mid-40 mph gusts. The 
depth of the stratus layer doesn't not look thick enough attm to 
lead to any drizzle/shower development. Temperatures by the 
afternoon Friday will surge into the upper 50s to lower 60s, but to 
some degree will also depend on cloud cover. 

SATURDAY-MONDAY: Medium range models are in much better agreement 
today, indicating that that western CONUS upper trough will move 
eastward, but likely split as it enters the Plains. The end result 
will push the highest risks for widespread rainfall over North 
Dakota and northern Minnesota. However, we'll still have an 
elongated surface boundary that develops over the western Dakotas 
and moves eastward into the Tri-State area by early Saturday 
morning. There should remain enough lift within the positively 
tilted upper trough, as well as moisture advecting ahead of the 
boundary to induce scattered showers along and east of the boundary 
into Saturday. Model soundings indicate very weak instability above 
the 700 mb surface, so not completely ruling out isolated lightning. 
Ensemble probabilities remain stable over the past 3 runs, 
suggesting a 40-60% probability for >0.10" of QPF into Saturday 
night. These lower probabilities fit well within the 25-75th 
percentile of the NBM which runs from 0 to 0.50". By Sunday a colder
